strengths: Extremely thorough empirical validation: PartCo is integrated into four different GCD baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) across three backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP) and 8 datasets (SSB fine-grained sets, generic sets, Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19), consistently improving over the corresponding baselines.

The framework is genuinely plug-and-play: it only adds a training-time auxiliary loss (Lpc) without modifying architecture or inference, and the overhead analysis (Table B) shows the added compute/memory cost is modest.

Extensive and well-designed ablations address many natural reviewer concerns: order-level ablation (1st/2nd/3rd), projection dimension, balancing factor, unsupervised loss contribution, comparison of PartCo labels against CUB's manually annotated ground-truth parts, foreground-masking-only baseline to isolate the effect of explicit part correspondence from simple background suppression, and comparison of PCA+DINOv2 label construction against a more expensive SD+DINOv2 alternative.
Additional robustness studies on unknown category number (K) estimation show PartCo-SelEx yields more accurate K estimates and remains robust even under poor K estimates.

Qualitative analyses (attention-map visualizations, per-class success/failure case study) provide interpretability and honest discussion of where the method helps (localized, part-dependent classes) and where it does not (globally/shape-defined classes, high intra-class variation).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea (aggregating patch tokens into pseudo-part clusters via PCA/k-means and applying a part-level contrastive loss) is conceptually similar to prior part-aware GCD works (SPTNet, APL, PartGCD) discussed in Related Work; the paper's main claimed innovation is largely a specific unsupervised labeling recipe layered onto standard contrastive losses.

The choice between 1st-order and 2nd-order part labels is dataset-type dependent (fine-grained vs. generic) and appears to require prior knowledge/manual selection rather than being learned or automatically determined, which limits the framework's claimed plug-and-play generality; the paper's guidance ('subtle intra-class differences' vs 'pronounced inter-class differences') is qualitative and not rigorously operationalized.

The heuristic used to select k* (number of part clusters) via a hand-crafted criterion (min pairwise centroid distance times cluster-size balance ratio) is somewhat ad hoc, with no theoretical justification or sensitivity analysis beyond the order-level ablation.

Gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal for the strongest baseline (e.g., PartCo-SelEx improves 'All' ACC on SSB DINOv2 by only +2.4% and even decreases 'Old' accuracy by -0.4%), suggesting diminishing returns when applied to already highly optimized methods, which tempers the generality of the claimed improvements.

Despite claims of 'setting new benchmarks,' several very recent 2025 methods (e.g., Hyp-SelEx, ConGCD-SelEx, NCGCD-SelEx) achieve comparable or sometimes better results than PartCo-SelEx on some datasets/splits (e.g., CUB 'Old' ACC), so the state-of-the-art claim is only partially substantiated.

No reported variance/standard deviation across multiple runs/seeds for the main results, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, particularly the smaller ones on generic datasets.

The method inherently requires ViT-style patch tokens, limiting applicability to non-transformer backbones, and the PCA-based label construction is somewhat sensitive to hyperparameters (e.g., objectness threshold τobj=0.6) without much sensitivity analysis provided in the main text.

strengths: Extremely extensive empirical validation: the method is integrated into four different GCD baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) across three backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP) and eight datasets (SSB fine-grained, generic, Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19), with consistent, non-trivial accuracy gains on the fine-grained benchmarks.

Thorough ablation studies covering order-level granularity, projection head dimensionality, supervised vs. unsupervised part loss, balancing factor, and robustness to erroneous K-estimation, which help substantiate the individual design choices.

The supplementary material includes valuable sanity checks that are often missing in similar papers: quantitative comparison of the constructed part labels against CUB ground-truth part annotations, a per-class success/failure analysis with qualitative explanation, and a computational overhead analysis showing the method adds only modest training cost and zero inference cost.

The method is framed and demonstrated as a lightweight, plug-and-play addition compatible with multiple existing GCD pipelines without modifying their architecture or inference path, which is practically attractive.
Clear, detailed writing with good figures illustrating the part-label construction pipeline and part correspondence loss.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is modest: the part-label construction is essentially a two-stage PCA + k-means pipeline on frozen DINOv2 features (a fairly standard unsupervised part/objectness discovery recipe), combined with a largely standard supervised/unsupervised contrastive loss applied to pooled patch features. The main contribution is an engineering combination of known components rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The choice between 1st-order and 2nd-order part labels is dataset-dependent and must be selected a priori based on whether the dataset is 'fine-grained' or 'generic' (the paper even states this selection is 'straightforward' based on visual inspection of inter/intra-class differences). This undermines the claimed plug-and-play generality, since for novel or ambiguous datasets this choice is not well automated and requires manual judgment, and extending to 3rd order is shown to actively hurt performance, suggesting the method is sensitive to this manual hyperparameter.

On generic benchmarks (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100) the improvements are small (often well under 1-2%), indicating the core motivating hypothesis (part correspondences aid discovery) is primarily validated on fine-grained data; the significance of the contribution for broader category discovery is therefore limited.

The claim of 'setting new benchmarks for GCD' is overstated: PartCo-SelEx is explicitly described as only 'on par' with the existing HypCD method rather than clearly superseding it, and several very recent SOTA methods (ConGCD, NCGCD) are not integrated with PartCo for direct comparison, making the overall ranking claim less convincing.

Several hyperparameters in the label-construction pipeline (objectness threshold τobj=0.6, number of seed labeled images M, k-means candidate range) are fixed without sensitivity analysis, leaving open questions about robustness to these choices across datasets of different scale/domain.

Reliance on explicit patch-token structure limits applicability to non-ViT backbones (acknowledged as a limitation), and the quality of the derived part-correspondence labels against CUB ground truth is only 77-81% accurate, implying a non-trivial amount of label noise is baked into the supervisory signal, with no deeper analysis of how this noise affects training dynamics beyond the ablations already shown.

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical evaluation across many datasets (CUB, Stanford-Cars, FGVC-Aircraft, CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100, Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19), multiple backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and multiple host GCD methods (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx), showing the proposed part-level correspondence loss is a genuinely plug-and-play module that yields consistent improvements over each baseline.

Thorough ablation studies addressing many natural questions: effect of 1st vs 2nd (vs 3rd) order part labels, output dimension of the projection head, value of the unsupervised part loss, sensitivity to the balancing factor, comparison of the PCA+DINOv2 label construction against a more expensive SD-DINOv2 alternative, and a useful 'foreground-masking only' control that isolates the contribution of explicit part correspondence beyond simple background suppression.

Quantitative validation of label quality against CUB's ground-truth part annotations (Table F), lending some credibility that the unsupervised part labels are semantically meaningful rather than arbitrary clusters.

Additional robustness analyses are valuable: behavior under inaccurate estimated category counts K (Table K), and qualitative/quantitative success-failure case analysis that gives an interpretable account of when part-level cues help (fine-grained, part-defined species) versus hurt (classes defined mainly by global shape or with high intra-class part variability).

Reasonable discussion of computational overhead (modest training-time/memory increase, no inference-time cost) and an honest limitations section identifying dependence on patch-token backbones and fixed-resolution correspondence.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: the core idea (PCA-based foreground/part discovery on frozen ViT patch tokens + supervised/unsupervised contrastive loss on aggregated part features) combines fairly standard self-supervised dense-correspondence and contrastive-learning techniques; the paper's own related work section notes concurrent works (APL, PartGCD) that pursue very similar part-aware GCD ideas, yet no direct head-to-head experimental comparison against these specific methods is run in the main benchmark table (only indirect comparison via reported numbers from their respective papers).

The strongest variant, PartCo-SelEx, does not uniformly set a new SOTA: on the SSB average it trails Hyp-SelEx (85.5 vs 86.0 'All' ACC) and is sometimes individually worse on Stanford-Cars, despite the abstract's claim of 'setting new benchmarks for GCD' and 'outperforming most existing methods' — the qualifier 'most' somewhat undercuts the strength of the claim and could be stated more precisely.

Selection between 1st-order and 2nd-order part labels is a manual, dataset-type-dependent heuristic (fine-grained vs. generic) rather than something the framework determines automatically; while the paper claims this choice is 'straightforward,' it still requires prior knowledge/assumptions about the dataset and is not learned or validated via a principled criterion at deployment time.

Gains on generic datasets (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100) are quite small (roughly +0.3% to +2.9%), suggesting the benefit of the proposed part-correspondence prior is concentrated on fine-grained benchmarks, which somewhat limits the generality of the significance claims despite the paper presenting results across both category types as equally important contributions.

Key hyperparameters in the label-construction pipeline (e.g., the objectness threshold τobj = 0.6) appear fixed without sensitivity analysis in the main paper, raising reproducibility/robustness questions about how brittle the part-label quality is to this choice across the diverse datasets evaluated.

The qualitative part-label visualizations (e.g., Fig. 4) show fairly sparse/noisy segmentations for several examples, and the Hungarian-matching validation against ground truth is performed only on CUB, leaving the quality of part correspondences on other datasets (cars, aircraft, generic images) largely unverified beyond downstream accuracy.
